doc.title: Clark Terry interviewed by Joe Williams and Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, May 19, 1995

title: Knowing the lyrics to play a tune meaningfully
summary: Terry says Hawkins, Webster, Tate and Lester Young knew the lyrics to every tune, which makes playing more expressive.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: There’s good guys and then there’s other people who care. Most definitely.
You know we’ve had a lot of that stuff happen. But it never, it does affect the music in one way —
Makes you keep on keepin’ on.
Yeah, but if you are doing a sad song, a sad thing, I think it puts another feeling into what you’re doing.
When you realize that they— for no reason —

Do you know this is a very, very important ingredient in the perpetuation of the craft of jazz, and this I got from, you just reiterated the same thing, that people have said, like Coleman Hawkins, Ben Webster, Budd Johnson, Buddy Tate, they all knew the lyrics to every tune that they played. And they said that if you —

That’s right. If you know the lyrics to the tune, you can express it in a much more meaningful manner then if you don’t know the lyrics. For instance, here’s a kid going to play “I Love You” well you says [sings] you wouldn’t say to a girl [angrily] I Love Ya. You think she’s going to believe that crap? She ain’t going for that. But she’ll sit there like, [sweetly sings] “I Love You” it might get across. It’s very, very important.
